descriptor.assumptions: Uses only the single most abundant alkali mole fractions as a proxy for total inorganic cation charge (divalent/other cations excluded); assumes osda_charge>0 for OSDA-containing gels and that formal charge equals the charge available for framework balancing; the 0.01 constant prevents division by zero for OSDA-free gels but makes the ratio explode toward very large values there, which trees handle as a saturated region. It is a composition proxy, not a measure of actual cation occlusion or charge-density matching in the product.
descriptor.expected_effect: As the ratio increases (inorganic cation charge >> OSDA charge), probability mass should shift from OSDA-templated frameworks (MFI, *BEA, MTW, BEC, MWW) toward alkali-templated small-pore/low-silica frameworks (LTA, CHA, FAU) and, at very large values (no or negligible OSDA), toward mineral/nitrate-templated or dense outcomes including Failed.
descriptor.falsification: If phase outcome is insensitive to this ratio within fixed OSDA and silica chemistry — e.g., the same OSDA at the same sda1 gives the same framework across a wide range of alkali loadings, or alkali-rich and OSDA-rich gels of equal ratio give different frameworks — the descriptor carries no phase-selection information and would show low split importance.
descriptor.hypothesis: The competition between inorganic alkali cations and the organic OSDA for charge-balancing and structure-directing roles steers which framework crystallizes: gels dominated by inorganic cations relative to OSDA charge favor small-pore, low-silica or OSDA-free-type frameworks (LTA, CHA, KFI-type, FAU, P1/GIS-type) or Failed (dense phases) when the inorganic excess is extreme, while gels where the OSDA charge dominates favor OSDA-templated high-silica frameworks (MFI, *BEA, MTW, MWW, BEC).
descriptor.mechanism: Framework anionic charge (from Al or Ge/F defects) must be balanced by cations in the gel. Alkali cations and OSDA cations occupy different voids and stabilize different building units (e.g., Na+ stabilizes sodalite/d6r-type units, K+ stabilizes d6r-containing small-pore frameworks, while bulky OSDA cations template larger cages and channels). When inorganic cation content greatly exceeds the available OSDA charge, inorganic cations dominate nucleation pathways toward alkali-templated topologies; when OSDA charge dominates, the OSDA templates its characteristic topology. Tree ensembles receive Na, K, ..., sda1 and osda_charge only as separate columns, so this ratio is not directly splittable without an explicit derived feature.
descriptor.name: inorganic_to_organic_cation_charge_ratio

descriptor.assumptions: The formula assumes all fluoride in the gel is bioavailable as mineralizing/occluded F⁻ (ignoring HF volatility, insoluble fluoride salts such as NaF/CaF2 precipitation, and speciation at different pH), and it treats sda1 as the only organic cation reservoir, ignoring inorganic cations and multi-OSDA systems (n_osda > 1) where charge competition is more complex. Because both F and sda1 are mole fractions of a normalized gel, the ratio also implicitly depends on the total concentration of the remaining species; the +0.01 constant avoids division by zero for hydroxide-route gels without fluoride or OSDA, mapping them to 0 (no-F) or a very large value (F without OSDA), respectively.
descriptor.expected_effect: As fluoride_to_osda_ratio increases from 0 toward ~1, phases that require defect-free or F⁻-stabilized cage frameworks become more likely (pure-silica *BEA/BEC, MTW, CHA-like cage phases) and the failure rate of pure-silica gels decreases; at very high ratios (>1, excess fluoride) selectivity shifts again toward small-pore high-silica phases (FER-type competitors diminish, cage-containing small-pore phases favored). At very low ratios (<0.3), amorphous products (Failed) and FER/MFI-type spacer phases become more likely.
descriptor.falsification: If the descriptor carries no phase-selective information, its split-based importance should be near zero and the confusion matrices conditioned on high vs. low F/sda1 bins should show the same framework distributions; conversely, the hypothesis is contradicted if low F/sda1 gels systematically yield cage-containing pure-silica phases or if excess-fluoride gels predominantly yield Failed without any small-pore crystalline products.
descriptor.hypothesis: The molar ratio of fluoride to OSDA in the gel controls which framework crystallizes in fluoride-mediated syntheses: gels with F⁻ roughly stoichiometric or in excess relative to OSDA charge (ratio >= ~1) favor phases where F⁻ is encapsulated as a counter-ion in small cages or where framework charge is compensated by F⁻ at defect sites (e.g., small-pore or cage-containing high-silica phases such as CHA, LEV, AST-like products, and excess-fluoride phases), whereas gels with sub-stoichiometric fluoride (ratio << 1) fail to crystallize pure-silica frameworks or shift selectivity toward bar/spacer phases such as FER or MFI-type products.
descriptor.mechanism: In fluoride media, F⁻ acts both as a mineralizer and as an inorganic structure-directing anion: it can reside inside small zeolite cages (e.g., D4R units) where it stabilizes double-ring units and allows syntheses at near-neutral pH with fewer connectivity defects. When fluoride is stoichiometric or in excess with respect to the OSDA cation, F⁻ competes with trivalent heteroatoms (Al, B) for charge compensation and stabilizes cage-containing frameworks via occluded F⁻; when fluoride is deficient, the OSDA cation must be balanced by framework [AlO4/2]⁻ or by silanol defects, which alters nucleation and shifts phase selectivity (e.g., pure-silica *BEA only forms at HF/OSDA = 1.0, pure-silica ZSM-5 at HF/OSDA = 0.25, FER at HF/OSDA <= 0.5, and no crystalline product at HF/OSDA = 0.13). Tree models receive F and sda1 only as separate mole fractions that are all normalized to sum to 1, so their ratio — the chemically meaningful stoichiometric quantity — is not directly accessible to a single split.

descriptor.assumptions: A single generic activation energy (Ea/R = 6000 K) is assumed for all gel chemistries; fluoride-mediated and low-temperature syntheses have different effective activation energies, so the absolute scale is a rough proxy rather than a physically exact rate integral. The formula assumes conventional hydrothermal heating (the dataset does not encode microwave or dry-gel-conversion routes, which change the effective dose at the same nominal time and temperature). Treats the whole synthesis as isothermal and ignores heating/cooling ramps and seeding, and does not capture time-dependent dissolution beyond a monotonically increasing dose.
descriptor.expected_effect: As arrhenius_thermal_dose increases from very small values, Failed (under-crystallized, amorphous) should first give way to metastable kinetic phases such as *BEA, MWW, AEI and UTL; at intermediate doses, well-defined OSDA-templated frameworks such as MFI and CHA dominate; at the largest doses, metastable large-pore phases should disappear in favor of thermodynamic phases (MOR, FER, dense/sodalite-like products) or Failed from dissolution, so the descriptor should be non-monotonically informative with distinct split regions per phase family.
descriptor.falsification: If the product label distribution at matched values of the thermal dose is no more coherent than at matched values of cryst_time or cryst_temp alone (i.e., the interaction adds no splits beyond those already available from the two raw columns), or if, for example, *BEA and MOR coexist indistinguishably across the whole dose range, the hypothesis is contradicted and the descriptor should be dropped.
descriptor.hypothesis: The product phase of a hydrothermal synthesis is governed not by temperature or time independently but by the integrated thermal severity of the treatment: gels receiving a low Arrhenius-weighted thermal dose tend to arrest at kinetic, OSDA-templated or metastable frameworks, while gels receiving a high thermal dose either transform to thermodynamically favored, denser phases or, for fragile frameworks such as SAPO-type and large-pore materials, partially dissolve and end as Failed or secondary-phase products. Because the classifier already receives cryst_time and cryst_temp as separate columns and tree ensembles cannot multiply them, this interaction is invisible to the current model.
descriptor.mechanism: Dissolution of amorphous precursors and framework rearrangement both follow Arrhenius kinetics with activation energies in the tens of kJ/mol range; the effective extent of hydrothermal reaction scales approximately as t * exp(-Ea/RT) with Ea/R ~ 6000 K used here as a generic zeolite crystallization activation energy (~50 kJ/mol). Metastable frameworks (e.g., *BEA, MWW, AEI, UTL) form early from the gel and are only metastable relative to the mother liquor: with increasing thermal dose, Ostwald-ripening and dissolution-reprecipitation convert them toward thermodynamically more stable phases (dense phases, quartz-like or sodalite-type products, or MOR/FER-type frameworks), or partially dissolve them (Failed). Conversely, an insufficient dose leaves the amorphous gel unconverted (Failed) or freezes in the first-nucleating metastable topology.
